conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Patel. I'll be part of your care team. You're here because of dizziness and unsteadiness again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I was doing okay after last time, but today I went for a walk and suddenly felt very woozy and fatigued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You didn’t fall, but you didn’t feel safe walking. Any numbness, weakness, or vision changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no numbness or vision problems. My wife says my right leg is dragging a bit, but I just notice my shoes make more noise when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s important. Given your history of CNS lymphoma, we need to check if there’s any change in your brain lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a PET scan after last discharge—was normal. Could this still be lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PET rules out systemic spread, but we still need an MRI to look closely at your brain. We’ll schedule that tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve been drinking more fluids—dry mouth lately—but no frequent urination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll check your electrolytes. No fever, chills, or weight loss?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. For now, just rest. A nurse will start your IV and draw some labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MRI from this morning shows the lesions in your brain have slightly increased in size, especially in the right occipital lobe and left internal capsule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Increased? Does that mean the lymphoma is back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning for recurrence. Other possibilities like methotrexate toxicity are less likely since your last dose was months ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s next? Another round of methotrexate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discussing with neuro-oncology. Given the progression, we’re planning to restart high-dose methotrexate, but at a higher dose—8 grams per square meter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Higher dose? Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take precautions—urinary alkalinization and leucovorin rescue—to protect your kidneys and bone marrow. It’s a standard protocol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When will it start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow, June 9th. We’ll admit you for close monitoring. We’ll also check your liver and kidney function closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day for your methotrexate infusion. We’ve started IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor for nausea, mouth sores, and low blood counts. Your liver enzymes might rise temporarily, but we expect them to come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll start that 24 hours after the infusion ends. It helps ‘rescue’ your healthy cells from the chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infusion went smoothly. You tolerated it well. We’ll keep the fluids going and monitor your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your potassium is low—2.7 this morning. We’re giving you supplements through the IV and orally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the aggressive hydration can flush out potassium. We’ll keep replacing it until it stabilizes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My balance still feels off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expected the dizziness to persist initially. We’re starting a short course of dexamethasone today—4 mg twice daily—to reduce brain swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids? I’ve had them before. Will I gain weight again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This is a low dose and short course—just until your next treatment. We’ll stop it before you go home to minimize side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your potassium is improving, up to 3.1. Your liver enzymes peaked yesterday but are starting to come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my balance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re walking more steadily today. The dexamethasone seems to be helping reduce the inflammation around the lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried I’d need a walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. You’re doing well. We’ll keep the dexamethasone for a few more days, then taper it off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Your symptoms have improved, labs are trending better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What’s next for treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get rituximab at the clinic next week. Then return here in two weeks for your next methotrexate dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a port?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll place one during your next admission. It’ll make the infusions easier and protect your veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your dizziness has improved, potassium is normal, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI showed progression of lymphoma, but the treatment is working. You’ll continue with rituximab and methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more steroids at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’ve stopped them. Just continue your aspirin and omeprazole. No magnesium citrate needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Patel. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. See you in the clinic next week. Call if you feel worse before then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’m ready when they are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you soon for your next treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.
